newsitem.title: USA: Muni issuers urged to look at corporate disclosure.
newsitem.headline: Muni issuers urged to look at corporate disclosure.

text.p: Municipal bond issuers wrangling with the new disclosure regulations can look to the corporate world for guidance on what sorts of events should be reported because they could affect the value of their securities, panelists at a municipal conference said Wednesday.

The municipal disclosure law (15C212) specifies only 11 "reportable events" that could affect the value of the bonds, leaving some issuers struggling to decide whether things such as potential changes in local tax ordinances or ongoing regulatory investigations should be disclosed in bond documents, panelists at the Bond Buyer Southeast Public Finance Conference in Atlanta said.
"It's hard to make a regulation one-size-fits all," said Marilyn Davis, district director for the National Association of Securities Dealers.

Earle Taylor, an attorney with the firm Kilpatrick Stockton LLP, said that generally anything that could affect the tax status of the bonds or the issuer's ability to repay the debt should be disclosed.
"You clearly don't have to disclose speculative things," Taylor said.
When in doubt, he said, "There is a very well developed body of law on the corporate side" that can provide guidance on what should be disclosed to investors.
"You're making the same sort of calls," Taylor said.

Charles Senatore, Southeast Regional Director of the Securities and Exchange Commission, agreed, reminding issuers that the municipal disclosure requirements are based on the same fundamental principles as the anti-fraud laws, which until recently have primarily been used to rein in the corporate securities world.
"There are well settled examples in other markets," Senatore agreed.

Senatore also said that when debating whether to disclose potential events such as a rate hike in the case of a water authority or the possibility of a lawsuit, "You sort of have to weigh the probability the event will occur."
Senatore dismissed the notion that his agency under Chairman Arthur Levitt has cracked down on the municipal industry in the last few years because it believes the industry to be wholly corrupt.
"There might be a weed here and there that might need to be plucked," Senatore said. However, he said, "Its certainly my opinon that the municipal marketplace is overwhelmingly honest."

The crackdown, especially in the areas of secondary market disclosure and prevention of pay-to-play practices, has been inspired by the shift from insitutional to individual investment in munis, Senatore said.
Individual investors now account for 65 to 70 percent of the market.
"The marketplace is not limited to the big boys who can take care of themselves," Senatore said. Because of that, "This element of the commission's program will continue with particular vigor."
